title: Conversational Spanish for Beginners
summary: By the end, learners can explain why a few Spanish phrases can be useful in Canada, greet someone and introduce themselves, use courtesy words and simple questions, count from one to ten and ask a basic shopping or direction question, and practise a short conversation — without treating this course as a language credential.

lessons.title: Why practise Spanish, and how to say hello
lessons.html:
Canada’s two official languages are English and French. Many other languages are also part of daily life. Statistics Canada, using the 2021 Census, reported that Spanish was the non-official language spoken by the most people in Canada (about 1,171,000 speakers). That figure comes from a Statistics Canada page released on January 22, 2025. Numbers can be updated in later censuses — check the live page.

You may hear Spanish at work, in a shop, at a community event, or from a neighbour. A few clear phrases can help you greet someone with respect. This course does not measure your language level and does not replace an English or French class.

Skills for Success communication means receiving, understanding, considering, and sharing information by speaking, listening, and interacting. Practise out loud. Listen for the rhythm. Spanish uses upside-down punctuation at the start of questions and exclamations: ¿ and ¡.

Useful greetings:

  • Hola — Hello
  • Buenos días — Good morning
  • Buenas tardes — Good afternoon
  • Buenas noches — Good evening or good night
  • Adiós — Goodbye
  • Hasta luego — See you later

Say Hola with a clear “o” sound, like “OH-lah.” Smile and speak at a calm pace. Spanish words and greetings can vary from country to country. These are widely understood starting points, not the only “correct” Spanish in the world.

lessons.title: Courtesy words and introducing yourself
lessons.html:
Courtesy words help a short conversation feel respectful.

  • Por favor — Please
  • Gracias — Thank you
  • De nada — You’re welcome
  • Perdón — Sorry, or “excuse me” if you bump into someone
  • Con permiso — Excuse me, when you need to pass by
  • Sí — Yes
  • No — No

To introduce yourself:

  • Me llamo [your name]. — My name is [your name].
  • ¿Cómo te llamas? — What is your name? (informal, with someone you know well)
  • ¿Cómo se llama usted? — What is your name? (more formal)
  • Mucho gusto. — Nice to meet you.
  • Igualmente. — Likewise.

Spanish has a more formal “you” (usted) and a more informal “you” (tú). With a customer, an older person, or someone you have just met, usted is often the safer, more respectful choice. With a close friend, tú is common. If you are not sure, start formal.

Try this out loud:

Hola. Me llamo Alex. ¿Cómo se llama usted? Mucho gusto.

Skills for Success communication includes adapting to your audience. A workplace or shop greeting is usually calmer and more formal than a chat with a close friend. Speak clearly. You do not need a perfect accent to be understood.

lessons.title: Simple questions and asking for help
lessons.html:
A good next step is asking how someone is, and asking for help when you do not understand.

  • ¿Cómo está usted? — How are you? (formal)
  • ¿Cómo estás? — How are you? (informal)
  • Bien, gracias. — Fine, thank you.
  • Más o menos. — So-so.
  • Mal. — Not well.
  • ¿Y usted? — And you?

When you need help with the language itself:

  • No entiendo. — I don’t understand.
  • Más despacio, por favor. — More slowly, please.
  • ¿Puede repetir, por favor? — Can you repeat that, please?
  • ¿Habla inglés? — Do you speak English?
  • Un poco. — A little.

Skills for Success communication includes listening with intention: pay attention, notice gestures, and ask questions to confirm what you heard. If you miss a word, it is better to say No entiendo than to guess and nod.

You can mix a Spanish courtesy word with a plain request: Perdón. No entiendo. Más despacio, por favor.

Practise the question mark at both ends: ¿ at the start and ? at the end. That written mark tells the reader a question is coming.

These phrases will not make you fluent. They give you a polite way to slow the conversation down and keep talking.

lessons.title: Numbers and useful everyday phrases
lessons.html:
Numbers help in a shop, a market, or when you are counting items.

  • uno — one
  • dos — two
  • tres — three
  • cuatro — four
  • cinco — five
  • seis — six
  • siete — seven
  • ocho — eight
  • nueve — nine
  • diez — ten

Useful phrases:

  • ¿Cuánto cuesta? — How much does it cost?
  • ¿Dónde está…? — Where is…?
  • el baño — the washroom
  • el agua — water
  • ayuda — help
  • ¿Me puede ayudar, por favor? — Can you help me, please?

Example: ¿Dónde está el baño, por favor? Example: ¿Cuánto cuesta? (you can point to the item)

In Canada you will still see prices in dollars. You do not need to change the currency words to use ¿Cuánto cuesta? The other person can show you the price or say it in English.

Say the numbers out loud several times. Pair them with your fingers if that helps you remember. Skills for Success communication includes speaking with clarity — a slow, clear uno, dos, tres is better than a rushed guess.

This lesson is phrase practice, not a math course and not shopping or tax advice.

lessons.title: Put a short conversation together
lessons.html:
Now join the pieces. Imagine you meet someone at a community hall or in a shop.

You: Buenos días. Me llamo Jordan. ¿Cómo está usted? Them: Bien, gracias. ¿Y usted? You: Bien, gracias. Mucho gusto. Them: Igualmente.

If you need something in the shop:

You: Hola. ¿Cuánto cuesta? ¿Me puede ayudar, por favor? If you get lost in the words: No entiendo. Más despacio, por favor. ¿Habla inglés?

Practise the whole exchange out loud two or three times. Record yourself on your phone if you like, then listen. Skills for Success communication includes both speaking with purpose and listening to understand.

Remember:

  • Spanish varies by country and region. A neighbour from Mexico, Spain, or Colombia may use a slightly different word. The greetings in this course are still a polite start.
  • Finishing this course does not make you fluent and is not a language credential.
  • Keep practising with a class, a tutor, a language-exchange partner, or short daily review. A real conversation class gives you listening practice this page cannot give.
  • Official languages in Canada are English and French. Learning a few Spanish phrases is extra help for daily life, not a replacement for English or French skills you may also be building.

Use the phrases you know. Be willing to say No entiendo. That is real communication.
